slides.title: Working with files
slides.content: Working with files • Up till now, we applied the bits of code we wrote to toy data • In real applications, we usually want to apply our code to data stored on the computer (and then save the processed data as well) • Today: the tools around the code • Find the right files: directories, paths, the command line • Read data from disk and write results • Reuse code: modules 2/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Files and directories
slides.content: Files and directories • Data is stored in files as a sequence of bytes • Files can be stored in directories (folders) • Directories can contain files and other directories • The file system is a tree structure • The location of a file is a path through this tree • Directories are useful to organize your files • No need to put everything in one big pile • Example: separate code, data, results 3/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Paths
slides.content: Paths • A path describes the location of a file • In the simplest case, just the filename is enough to refer to a file in the same directory as your program/notebook: • example.txt • If a file is somewhere else, need to include directories: • data/example.txt • data/novels/19thcentury/austen/emma.txt • Use ‘..’ (two dots) to refer to the parent directory • NB: Windows uses \ instead of / • However, this causes problems: use / in Python 4/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Absolute and relative paths
slides.content: Absolute and relative paths • An absolute path starts at the root of the file system • /home/tim/project/data/emma.txt (Linux) • /Users/tim/project/data/emma.txt (Mac) • C:/Users/tim/project/data/emma.txt (Windows) • A relative path starts from the working directory: the directory your program or notebook is running in • data/emma.txt • ../data/emma.txt • Absolute paths only work on your computer; relative paths work for everyone who has the same directory structure • Prefer relative paths in your code 5/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Where am I?
slides.content: Where am I? • A relative path is only meaningful if you know your working directory • Ask Python: In: import os In: os.getcwd() Out: '/home/tim/project/notebooks' • For a notebook, the working directory is normally the directory the notebook is in • FileNotFoundError usually means: the path is correct, but relative to a different directory 6/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Try it: paths
slides.content: Try it: paths project/ notebooks/ analysis.ipynb data/ novels/ emma.txt results/ • The notebook analysis.ipynb is running in notebooks/ • Which path do you use to read emma.txt? • Which path do you use to write counts.txt into results/? 7/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Anatomy of a path
slides.content: Anatomy of a path A path like data/novels/austen/emma.txt has several parts: Directory data/novels/austen/ Filename emma.txt Base name emma Extension .txt • We often need to extract or manipulate these parts • E.g. to sort files by name, or to construct an output filename from an input filename • Python provides the os.path module for this 8/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Manipulating paths with os.path
slides.content: Manipulating paths with os.path In: from os.path import basename, splitext, join, exists In: basename('data/novels/austen/emma.txt') Out: 'emma.txt' In: splitext('emma.txt') Out: ('emma', '.txt') In: join('data', 'novels', 'emma.txt') Out: 'data/novels/emma.txt' In: exists('data/novels/emma.txt') Out: True • basename: removes the directory part • splitext: splits into name and extension • join: builds a path (with the right separator for your system) • exists: check before you open 9/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Reading a file
slides.content: Reading a file with open('document.txt') as in_file: for line in in_file: print(line) • with statement automatically closes your file when you’re done • We iterate over the file line by line • Each line is a string (including the newline character '\n') • Use line.strip() to remove leading/trailing whitespace and newlines • in_file.read() reads the entire file as a single string 10/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Reading and writing
slides.content: Reading and writing with open('document.txt') as in_file: with open('processed_document.txt', 'w') as out_file: for line in in_file: line = line.replace('a', 'b') out_file.write(line) • Second argument to open: the mode • 'r': reading (default) • 'w': writing (overwrites an existing file!) • 'a': appending • 'b': binary data (default is text) • write takes one string and does not add a newline: add '\n' yourself • Note: we can only read and process files in plain text format ('txt') • Loading something like Word or PDF files will not work because those are encoded in a binary format 11/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Text encoding
slides.content: Text encoding • A text file is represented using a particular text encoding • Particularly important for non-Western characters, or e.g. emojis • You need to use the correct encoding when reading and saving your text 12/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Text encoding
slides.content: Text encoding • Always use the Unicode character set with UTF-8 encoding • Which is the default for Python (and many other programs) • Might be more problematic with older datasets or Windows programs 13/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Text encoding: specifying the encoding
slides.content: Text encoding: specifying the encoding • If you try to load a text in a different encoding, Python will raise an error • Solution: specify the encoding explicitly # This will cause an error if the file # is not in UTF-8: with open('document_latin1.txt') as in_file: for line in in_file: print(line) # UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't # decode byte 0xe9 ... # Fix: specify the encoding with open('document_latin1.txt', encoding='latin1') as in_file: for line in in_file: print(line) 14/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: The command line
slides.content: The command line • Textual interface that takes commands for the computer’s operating system as lines of text • Also called: terminal, shell, console • Linux and Mac: Terminal (unix shell) • Windows: Anaconda Prompt or PowerShell (different commands) • Useful for file management, and to run programs (e.g. python) • Many tools in research only exist as command line tools • Note: the command line is not Python; it is a separate language 15/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Basic commands
slides.content: Basic commands unix shell Windows print working directory pwd cd list directory ls dir change directory cd data cd data go to parent directory cd .. cd .. make directory mkdir results mkdir results copy, move/rename, remove cp, mv, rm copy, move, del show first lines of a file head emma.txt more emma.txt run a Python script python script.py python script.py • Paths work exactly as in Python: relative to the working directory, .. for the parent • Tab completes file names; the up arrow repeats the previous command 16/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: The command line from a notebook
slides.content: The command line from a notebook • In a notebook, prepend an exclamation mark (!) to run a command on the command line !ls data !head data/emma.txt !wget http://example.org/corpus.zip !unzip corpus.zip • Each ! command runs in a fresh shell: !cd data has no lasting effect • To change the working directory of the notebook itself: %cd data • Jupyter commands that start with % are called magic commands 17/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Try it: the command line
slides.content: Try it: the command line project/ notebooks/ analysis.ipynb data/ novels/ emma.txt results/ • You open a terminal in project/. Which commands do you type to: • list the files in novels/ • move into notebooks/ • from there, show the first lines of emma.txt 18/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: From files to tools
slides.content: From files to tools • We’ve already used os.path, and we’ll soon use glob and pickle • These are all examples of modules: reusable collections of code • Modules allow us to go beyond Python’s builtin functionality • Let’s look at how importing works 19/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Importing modules
slides.content: Importing modules To go beyond builtin functionality, use import: # import whole module: import <module> # or import a specific part: from <module> import <function> 20/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Importing modules
slides.content: Importing modules To go beyond builtin functionality, use import: # import whole module: import <module> # or import a specific part: from <module> import <function> In: import math In: math.pi Out: 3.141592653589793 In: from math import sqrt In: sqrt(16) 4.0 Matter of preference/convention which you use: • math.pi: clear that pi comes from math module • sqrt: more convenient usage 20/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: The Python standard library
slides.content: The Python standard library • ‘Batteries included’ • Many different modules with useful functions • See https://docs.python.org/3/library/index.html • Today: • os.path: manipulate paths • glob: find files by pattern • pickle: save Python objects to disk 21/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Finding files by pattern
slides.content: Finding files by pattern • Before we can read files, we often need to find them • globbing: matching a set of files with a search pattern • The most common operators are: • * meaning “match zero or more characters” • ? meaning “match exactly one character” 22/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Finding files by pattern
slides.content: Finding files by pattern • Before we can read files, we often need to find them • globbing: matching a set of files with a search pattern • The most common operators are: • * meaning “match zero or more characters” • ? meaning “match exactly one character” Example: In: from glob import glob In: glob('scripting_practical?.ipynb') Out: ['scripting_practical1.ipynb', 'scripting_practical2.ipynb', 'scripting_practical3.ipynb',] In: glob('data/*.txt') Out: ['data/austen.txt', 'data/dickens.txt', 'data/joyce.txt'] • The same patterns work on the command line: ls data/*.txt 22/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Processing multiple files
slides.content: Processing multiple files from glob import glob for filename in glob('data/*.txt'): with open(filename) as in_file: text = in_file.read() word_count = len(text.split()) print(f'{filename}: {word_count} words') • This is a common pattern: find files, then process them one by one • glob returns the files in arbitrary order: use sorted(glob(...)) if the order matters 23/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Sorting with a key function
slides.content: Sorting with a key function In: names = ['Charlie', 'Alice', 'Bob'] In: sorted(names) Out: ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'] 24/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Sorting with a key function
slides.content: Sorting with a key function In: names = ['Charlie', 'Alice', 'Bob'] In: sorted(names) Out: ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'] # Sort by length instead of alphabetically: In: sorted(names, key=len) Out: ['Bob', 'Alice', 'Charlie'] 24/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Sorting with a key function
slides.content: Sorting with a key function In: names = ['Charlie', 'Alice', 'Bob'] In: sorted(names) Out: ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'] # Sort by length instead of alphabetically: In: sorted(names, key=len) Out: ['Bob', 'Alice', 'Charlie'] • The key argument: a function that is applied to each item before comparing • key=len: sort by the length of each string • Any function will do, also your own: sorted(filenames, key=get_year) • reverse=True: sort from high to low 24/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Saving Python objects with pickle
slides.content: Saving Python objects with pickle • What if we want to save a Python object (e.g. a dictionary or a list)? • pickle: module for saving Python objects directly to disk translation_dictionary = {'red': 'rouge', 'green': 'vert'} import pickle with open('translations.pickle', 'wb') as out_file: pickle.dump(translation_dictionary, out_file) with open('translations.pickle', 'rb') as in_file: my_translations = pickle.load(in_file) my_translations Out: {'red': 'rouge', 'green': 'vert'} • Binary mode ('wb', 'rb'): not human-readable, but preserves the exact Python object; useful to save intermediate results 25/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Installing packages
slides.content: Installing packages • Most of these are part of Anaconda distribution; already installed! • (Exceptions: Spacy, gensim) • Install conda packages with Anaconda Navigator • Install other packages with pip (more advanced, much more packages) • Note: pip is a command line tool; in notebook, you can execute it with: • %pip install spacy 27/30 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be
